unknowns.answer: Contents: Read-only plus Metadata: Read-only. Insufficient permissions give a 403 ('Resource not accessible by integration'). X-Accepted-GitHub-Permissions is returned in REST responses generally, so it is a hint only. Whether Metadata is mandatory is not stated.

The token reaches the intersection of what the user and the app can access. Listing uses GET /user/installations and GET /user/installations/{id}/repositories. Install link: https://github.com/apps/APP-NAME/installations/new. The not-installed error and install rights moved to U-10 and U-11.
Device flow as before. HTTP 200 + error is stated only for the pending phase. Other statuses and step-1 errors are not stated, so the client reads error from the body whatever the status.

Refresh needs no client_secret for a token 'generated using the device flow' (worded per token). Whether a refreshed token still counts is not stated; the two-refreshes day-one check is in the BRIEF. Each refresh rotates both tokens. bad_refresh_token means a new sign-in.

No secret means no DELETE /applications/*. /credentials/revoke is for exposed credentials. A revoked token gets 401 Bad Credentials; the status for an expired token is not stated. The ten-token rule is stated for OAuth apps only.
Prefixes ghu_ (user) and ghr_ (refresh), among others. Lengths and character sets are not stated. Used only to validate the token response's shape; redaction is exact-value per vault entry.
commits, contents, trees, blobs, tarball and zipball all accept user tokens with Contents read.
Settings unchanged. A public app can be installed and authorized by anyone; a private one only on the owning account. 'Any account' = public is an inference (E-03 line 93, E-14 line 20).

2022-11-28 is supported until March 10, 2028; 2026-03-10 has no end date. A retired version returns 410 Gone, with Deprecation/Sunset headers beforehand; an unknown version returns 400. Keep 2022-11-28 for the sign-in work.

A private resource the request cannot reach returns 404, not 403. GitHub's 404 checklist for user tokens: app permission, user permission, app has repository access (installed), user has access, updated permissions approved. SAML needs an active session (status not stated). The client cannot tell the causes apart, so its message lists them. Field observation of three cases is a non-blocking day-one check.

Anyone can install on their own account and owners on their organization. Repository admins can install for repositories they administer when the app requests no org permission (unless owners restrict it). Members and outside collaborators trigger an owner request (Install and request / Request). The app manager role cannot install. A collaborator on another person's personal repository must ask that person (a reading of the option list).

User-token requests take the signed-in user's own 5,000 requests/hour, shared across apps and tokens, plus secondary limits including 2,000 OAuth token requests/hour for GitHub Apps (numbers from the prior project's REST rate-limit capture). Exceeding a limit gives 403/429: primary with x-ratelimit-remaining 0; secondary with a message and retry-after only if present, else wait at least 1 minute.

Settings > Integrations: Applications > Authorized GitHub Apps tab > Revoke (no direct URL stated). Only the authorizing person can revoke; org owners can uninstall instead. Revoking revokes the tokens, which then get 401.

Owners of installing accounts are notified and must approve; until then the installation keeps its old permissions. Authorized-only users are not notified. A request can 404 until updated permissions are approved.

GET /user works with GitHub App user tokens and needs no permission; statuses 200/304/401/403; the example carries login and id. Public vs private response for app tokens is not stated; login is expected and checked on day one.

Whether the device flow's 50 submissions/hour per application (stated for OAuth apps) applies to a GitHub App, per app, is not stated on any GitHub App page. Day one: the product owner asks GitHub Support (or measures past 50 in an hour with a test account) and records the answer in U-16. Until then, assume per-app, give expired_token a message that mentions possible limiting, and record it as a product risk.

findings.problem: The 403 mapping leaves out the only 403 cause GitHub documents, insufficient permissions. It lists two causes GitHub never ties to 403: app not installed (documented as a 404 cause) and SAML (status not stated). The lead's F-3 fix said that once rate limits are excluded, a 403 is treated as a missing permission. The round-2 text dropped that meaning entirely.
findings.evidence: BRIEF.md lines 374-376: '403 otherwise -> forbidden ... no access, app not installed, SAML session needed, or a secondary limit GitHub did not label'. E-04 capture line 75: 'If your app makes a REST API request with insufficient permissions, the API will return a `403` response.' E-15 capture line 108: 'Resource not accessible by integration' means 'your token has insufficient permissions'. E-15 lines 65-70 put 'The GitHub App has access to any repositories...' on the 404 checklist, not under 403. E-01 line 34 gives no status for SAML. The round-1 F-3 fix text: 'Only after that treat a 403 as a missing permission'.
findings.fix: In Decision step 3, put this cause first: 'the app or your account lacks a permission this read needs, for example an owner has not yet approved updated permissions' (E-04 line 75, E-15 lines 70 and 108). Use the body message 'Resource not accessible by integration' as GitHub's documented signal for it, and keep X-Accepted-GitHub-Permissions as a hint only. Keep 'app not installed' and 'SAML' only as labelled possibilities that GitHub does not state for 403. Add a Next-steps test: a 403 with that body and no rate-limit headers.

findings.problem: The SAML remedy leaves out half of what the capture says. GitHub tells the user to start a SAML session and then reauthorize. The brief tells them only to start a session. A user in a SAML organization who follows MoonAliza's message would start a session, retry with the same token, and could fail again with no next step.

findings.problem: The main recovery path for a repository the app is not installed on is: 404, install link, user installs, retry. Record whether each read works without a new sign-in and how soon. Until then, the install message adds: 'if it still fails after installing, sign in again'.

findings.problem: The brief dismisses the secondary limit of 2,000 OAuth access-token requests per hour by counting refreshes per user. It does not consider that device-flow polls are, in GitHub's own words, access-token requests to the same endpoint. If the limit counts per app, it caps sign-ins and refreshes across all MoonAliza users. Separately, the rate-limit-first rule covers REST reads only: poll and refresh calls to github.com/login/oauth/access_token have no rate-limit handling, and nothing says a rate-limited refresh must keep the vault.
findings.evidence: BRIEF.md lines 327-328: 'not stated; MoonAliza refreshes about three times a day per user'. Prior rate-limit capture (docs/research/2026-10-12-app-sign-in/research/raw/2026-10-12-rate-limits-for-the-rest-api-github-docs-github-4a04a6e2.md) line 95: 'No more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour are allowed for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.' E-01 line 132 defines `interval` as the wait 'before you can make a new access token request (`POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token`)'. At the default 5 s interval and 900 s expiry (E-01 lines 131-132), one sign-in can make up to 180 polls. The error mapping (BRIEF.md lines 368-372) is written for read_github only.
findings.fix: Label it like U-16: whether the limit counts per app, and whether device-flow polls count toward it, is not stated. Add both questions to U-16's GitHub Support step and record the per-app case as a product risk. Apply the rate-limit-first classification to poll and refresh responses as well: 429; 403 with x-ratelimit-remaining 0; retry-after. A rate-limited refresh keeps the vault and fails the call as GITHUB_RATE_LIMIT. Add Next-steps tests for both.

findings.problem: Refresh failures are not fully specified, and E-15 is misread on expired tokens. (a) The brief says E-15 lists expired tokens as a 404 cause only for PATs and installation tokens. E-15 also lists them for OAuth-app user access tokens, and E-01 says a GitHub App user token is a type of OAuth token. (b) The brief says 'The Decision handles either' a 401 or a 404 for an expired token, but the 404 path never refreshes. That claim holds only if no call ever goes out with an expired token, and the brief does not say what a call does when its pre-check refresh fails for a reason other than bad_refresh_token (network, 5xx, rate limit). (c) 'Read `error` from the body whatever the status' is stated for the device flow only. The status of bad_refresh_token is not stated, so a client that checks res.ok first could treat it as transient and never clear the vault.
findings.evidence: DISCOVERY.md U-5 (line 29): 'E-15 lists expired tokens among 404 causes for personal access tokens and installation tokens only, lines 53-64'. The E-15 row in EVIDENCE.md and BRIEF.md lines 237-239 say the same. E-15 capture line 75, under 'If you are using an OAuth app user access token': 'The token has not been expired or revoked.' E-01 line 36: 'A user access token is a type of OAuth token.' BRIEF.md lines 316-317: '(401, or 404 on a private repository). The Decision handles either.' Decision 404 path: lines 377-382. Read-error-from-body rule: lines 350-352, sign-in only. E-01 line 275 gives no HTTP status for bad_refresh_token.
findings.fix: Correct 'only' to include E-15 line 75 (OAuth-app user tokens), noting it is an analogy, not a statement about GitHub App tokens. In the Decision, state that refresh responses are read for `error` whatever the HTTP status, and record 'status of refresh errors: not stated'. State that a call whose pre-check refresh fails transiently fails with a retriable error, keeps the vault, and never sends an expired token; that is what makes 'handles either' true. Also have the 401-triggered refresh join the same single-flight, and skip it when the vault's access token is no longer the one that got the 401 (rotation, E-02 line 36). Add tests for a transient refresh failure and for bad_refresh_token returned with a non-200 status.
